paper_did: Developed a combined in situ plasmonic nanospectroscopy and mass spectrometry (QMS) setup for gas‐phase CO oxidation at high temperature and atmospheric pressure.
Fabricated Au@SiO2–Pt hybrid nanostructures featuring polycrystalline Pt nanoparticles (~20 × 70 nm) grown on an inert, SiO2‐encapsulated Au nanoantenna to serve as both catalyst and optical sensor.
Conducted CO oxidation experiments by varying the CO/O2 ratio (αCO) and simultaneously monitoring the LSPR spectral shift (Δλ) and CO2 production to reveal kinetic phase transitions and hysteresis.
Tested the thermal and chemical stability of the nanostructures through annealing and reaction treatments and characterized the nanoparticle grain structure using TEM and SEM.
paper_reported: Identified a distinct kinetic phase transition in CO oxidation where the plasmonic nanospectroscopy signal (Δλ) abruptly changes as the Pt surface switches from an oxygen‐covered state to a CO‐covered state.

Found that individual Pt nanoparticles exhibit notably different bistable kinetic behaviors—with hysteresis and sharp phase transitions—attributed to variations in grain structure and surface faceting.
Demonstrated that ensemble averaging of many nanoparticles leads to a broadened and smeared reaction response compared to the sharper transitions observed on single-particle measurements.
paper_proposed: Suggested that the in situ plasmonic nanospectroscopy technique can be extended to study additional processes such as alloying, surface segregation, and further structure–activity relationships in nanoparticle catalysts.

paper_did: Developed an HEO impurity model based on DFT calculations to quantify the effects of random multi‐element mixing on local strain, mixing enthalpy, and adsorption energies at active metal sites.
Synthesized equimolar high‐entropy spinel oxides (comprising Co, Fe, Ni, Cr, and Mn) via a rapid sol‐flame method and deposited them as thin films on FTO/glass substrates.

Characterized the synthesized catalysts using XRD, TEM, SEM, STEM with EDS elemental mapping, XPS, XAS, and EELS to confirm the pure spinel structure, nanoparticle morphology, homogeneous elemental distribution, and surface as well as bulk oxidation states.

Measured electrochemical oxygen evolution reaction (OER) performance in alkaline electrolyte by recording polarization curves, Tafel slopes, electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS), and durability tests as well as assessing the electrochemical surface area (ECSA), and compared these results between HEO and lower‐entropy oxide analogues.
paper_reported: The high‐entropy spinel oxide (HEO) exhibited superior OER activity with the lowest overpotential (~307 mV at 10 mA cm⁻²), a smaller Tafel slope, higher electrical conductivity, and enhanced stability (minimal overpotential increase over extended operation) compared to lower‐entropy counterparts.

DFT calculations and the impurity model revealed that multi‐element mixing induces strain effects near the active sites, which in turn lead to a broader distribution of adsorption energies for key intermediates (*OH and *O), thereby shifting some active sites closer to optimal volcano‐plot conditions.

Surface analysis (via XPS, EELS, and XAS) indicated that the HEO catalysts naturally exhibit a favorable oxidation state distribution (for example, higher Co³⁺/Co²⁺ and enhanced Fe²⁺ presence) and evolve into partly oxyhydroxide (MOOH) phases during OER, which contribute to the observed high activity and durability.
paper_proposed: Future work should further unravel the interplay between elemental mixing, induced strain, and surface oxidation state evolution to optimize OER catalyst performance.

The paper suggests exploring variations in the catalyst composition—such as fixing a subset of metal cations and varying the fifth one (e.g., testing Cr, V, Cu, Zn, W)—to systematically tune adsorption energetics and identify the optimal active site configuration.

There is an implicit proposal to utilize the insights from the HEO impurity model and the experimentally observed benefits of mixing-induced strain to guide the rational design of next-generation, non-noble metal OER catalysts.

paper_reported: Surface oxidation converts a significant amount of surface Ni0 into Ni(OH)2 (with some residual Ni0) and leads to a synergistic Ni/Ni(OH)2 interface that boosts intrinsic HER activity.

Employing combined experimental and computational approaches to deepen the understanding of how surface oxidation and interface structures influence HER kinetics, which may include future studies on durability and extended cycling performance.

Performed electrochemical measurements for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in 1 M KOH at room temperature using a three‐electrode cell, including cyclic voltammetry with both cathodic HER testing and anodic oxidation cycling.

paper_did: Fabricated nanoparticle-based transition metal catalysts (Ag, Au, Pd, Sn, and Cu) via sputter deposition onto a carbon-based gas diffusion electrode (GDE) with controlled catalyst layer morphology and nominal thickness (~100 nm).

Operated a controlled three-compartment electrochemical cell using a common cell architecture with fixed current densities (10, 50, 100, and 200 mA/cm²) and two electrolytes (1 M KHCO₃ and 1 M KOH), with CO₂ fed under regulated gas flow.

Conducted 1-hour electrolysis experiments (and duplicates) with comprehensive monitoring including chronopotentiometry, online GC analysis of gas products, and post-reaction characterization (SEM, XPS, and profilometry) to assess catalyst activity, selectivity, and stability.
paper_reported: Ag catalysts demonstrated high CO selectivity (approximately 80–90%) over a range of current densities but exhibited the formation of large, K/O-rich salt deposits (likely potassium carbonate) on the surface, which could compromise long-term performance.

Au catalysts showed an intrinsic limiting CO partial current density (~72 mA/cm²) with a decline in CO selectivity and increased H₂ evolution at higher current densities, independent of catalyst layer thickness.

Pd catalysts reached a lower CO production plateau (~50 mA/cm²) and tended toward increased hydrogen evolution with significant morphological changes, while Sn catalysts achieved high formate selectivity but suffered from poor stability and dissolution (especially in alkaline media).

Cu catalysts exhibited significant in situ morphological restructuring (e.g., formation of nanoneedles and cubic facets) with product distributions shifting toward enhanced multicarbon (C₂⁺) products, such as ethylene, at elevated current densities.
paper_proposed: Further research to determine whether the observed limiting current density for CO production on Au (and Pd) is intrinsic to the material or influenced by operational conditions.

Exploration of catalyst stabilization strategies, particularly for unstable materials like Sn, including the potential use of alloying, binding agents, ionomers, or co-catalysts to mitigate catalyst loss and degradation.

An in‐depth investigation of how catalyst morphology and the local reaction environment under high current density conditions affect product selectivities and overall catalyst durability for industrially relevant CO₂ reduction.

pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: the paper’s observation that the surface state (CO- versus O-covered) governs catalytic kinetics, extending it by introducing a support modification that actively supplies oxygen.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis innovates by incorporating an ultrathin oxygen-active overlayer designed to facilitate oxygen spillover onto Pt, an approach not explored in the original study which purposefully used an inert SiO2 encapsulation to avoid metal-support interactions.

fields.hypothesis: Catalytic activity and durability in Pt-based CO oxidation can be enhanced by engineering an ultrathin oxygen-donating overlayer (e.g., CeO2) on the Pt nanoparticle, which acts as an internal oxygen reservoir promoting oxygen spillover. This modification sustains an oxygenated surface state and reduces CO poisoning despite the high reaction temperatures.
fields.material_initial_state: Au@SiO2–Pt hybrid nanostructures where Pt nanoparticles are supported on an inert SiO2 encapsulated Au nanoantenna.
fields.intervention: Deposit an ultrathin, conformal layer (1–2 nm thick) of an oxygen-active metal oxide such as CeO2 on top of the Pt nanoparticles. The layer should be engineered to be sufficiently transparent (or discontinuous) so as not to interfere with the plasmonic readout.
fields.conditions: CO oxidation reaction in the gas phase at atmospheric pressure and temperatures between 503 and 623 K.
fields.structural_mediator: Metal–oxide interface that facilitates oxygen spillover by supplying reactive oxygen species to the Pt surface.
fields.mechanism: An oxygen-active overlayer like CeO2 can generate mobile oxygen species through its redox cycling and supply them via spillover to the Pt active sites. This maintains an oxygen-rich surface even under CO-rich conditions, curbing the poisoning effect by ensuring that the catalyst surface remains active for CO oxidation. The carefully engineered thin layer minimizes disruption of the plasmonic signal from the underlying Au nanoantenna.
fields.predicted_outcome: Pt catalysts with the CeO2 overlayer will display a plasmonic signature indicating a more oxygen-like surface state (smaller or delayed Δλ shifts toward CO poisoning) and will produce higher, more stable CO2 rates compared to catalysts on inert supports.
fields.baseline: Conventional Au@SiO2–Pt nanostructures with an inert support that exhibit pronounced kinetic bistability and CO poisoning under comparable reaction conditions.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected when the CeO2 overlayer is ultrathin and well-controlled; excessively thick or non-uniform layers could compromise plasmonic sensing and block active sites.
fields.uncertainty: It remains to be determined how the overlayer’s thickness and continuity precisely balance oxygen spillover with optical transparency; the quantitative improvements in activity may vary with deposition conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of Au@SiO2–Pt nanostructures: one with an ultrathin CeO2 overlayer and one without (control). Under identical CO oxidation conditions, measure the plasmonic response and CO2 production rates.
measurements: LSPR peak shifts (Δλ) to monitor the catalyst surface state
Temporal stability of the plasmonic signal during CO oxidation cycles
CO2 production rates via QMS to assess overall activity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CeO2-modified catalysts do not show a statistically significant delay or reduction in CO poisoning indicators (lower Δλ shift) and do not produce higher, more stable CO2 formation compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: the paper’s mechanistic proposal that the unique core–shell structure in Cu/N:C catalysts enables a non-free-radical pathway, enhancing selectivity.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes directly manipulating the oxide shell thickness via heat treatment to elucidate its role in selectivity, a parameter that the paper observed but did not systematically control or optimize.

fields.hypothesis: The catalytic selectivity in transition-metal catalyzed oxidation is governed by the thickness of the active oxide shell on the metal particles. For example, in Cu catalysts, a controlled thin Cu2O shell over a CuO core creates an optimal interface for the surface reaction of adsorbed hydroperoxide intermediates, suppressing free-radical release and enhancing selectivity.
fields.material_initial_state: Cu/N:C catalysts prepared by standard impregnation/thermal treatment (typically at 300 °C) that produce a CuO–Cu2O core–shell structure.
fields.intervention: Vary the post-impregnation heat treatment temperature to control the thickness of the Cu2O shell. For instance, compare catalysts treated at a slightly lower temperature (e.g., 250 °C) versus the standard 300 °C and possibly a higher temperature (e.g., 350 °C).
fields.conditions: Use the same cyclohexene oxidation reaction conditions (70 °C, 10 bar O2, specific solvent and stirring rates) for all catalyst batches.
fields.structural_mediator: The controlled thickness of the Cu2O shell on the supported particles, which defines the density and accessibility of labile surface sites that mediate the oxygen transfer and subsequent hydroperoxide conversion.
fields.mechanism: A thinner Cu2O shell is expected to have a higher density of reactive surface sites that allow for rapid rearrangement of adsorbed cyclohexenyl hydroperoxide to form the ketone product, whereas too thick a shell may reduce site accessibility. This moderation in shell thickness can tilt the balance from a free-radical pathway (associated with over-oxidation) to a selective surface-bound mechanism.
fields.predicted_outcome: There will be an optimal heat treatment temperature at which the catalyst exhibits maximal selectivity to the ketone product (2-cyclohexene-1-one) and reduced formation of over-oxidation products; catalysts treated at temperatures deviating from this optimum will show lower selectivity.
fields.baseline: The catalyst performance as reported in the study prepared at 300 °C, which produced a certain core–shell structure correlating with high selectivity.
fields.boundary: This mechanism should hold under the mild reaction conditions used (70 °C, 10 bar O2) and for catalysts where only thermal treatment is varied. Extreme temperatures that fundamentally alter particle size or support structure would fall outside this boundary.
fields.uncertainty: The precise optimal shell thickness and the quantitative change in selectivity are not predetermined and must be established experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three batches of Cu/N:C catalysts at different post-impregnation heat treatment temperatures (e.g., 250 °C, 300 °C, and 350 °C). Characterize the oxide shell thickness using XPS/XRD and test each in cyclohexene oxidation.
measurements: Determine conversion and selectivity (yield of ketone vs. over-oxidation products)
Correlate oxide shell thickness with catalytic performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If changes in heat treatment (and thus oxide shell thickness) do not result in systematic variations in catalytic selectivity (with no identifiable optimum), then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration that oxide formation at the Mo2C surface is the key detrimental factor for CO2RR activity.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a protective coating strategy to physically inhibit oxidation while preserving catalyst functionality — a route not investigated in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A deliberately applied ultrathin carbon protective overlayer on Mo2C will act as a diffusion barrier against oxygen, thereby mitigating the formation of passivating surface oxides and preserving the catalyst’s intrinsic CO2RR activity in aqueous media.
fields.material_initial_state: Air-exposed Mo2C films that rapidly form MoO2-like surface oxides upon immersion in aqueous electrolytes.
fields.intervention: Deposit an ultrathin, conductive carbon layer (via chemical vapor deposition or pyrolysis of a carbon precursor) atop the Mo2C catalyst immediately after synthesis, ensuring minimal thickness to allow electron transfer while hampering oxygen infiltration.
fields.conditions: Aqueous electrolyte (e.g., 0.1 M KHCO3 at pH ~6.9) with typical cathodic polarization conditions for CO2 reduction.
fields.structural_mediator: A conformal nanometer-scale carbon film that adheres to the Mo2C surface and modulates the interfacial chemistry by limiting oxygen diffusion without significantly impeding charge transport.
fields.mechanism: The protective carbon overlayer is expected to prevent or slow the ingress of oxygen species during exposure to aqueous electrolyte. This reduction in oxide formation maintains the active carbide surface that is predicted (by prior DFT studies and indicated in the paper) to have favorable adsorption properties for CO2 and its intermediates, thereby shifting the reaction selectivity away from HER toward CO2RR.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated Mo2C that rapidly forms HER-active oxide films, the coated catalyst should show a markedly thinner oxide film (as measured by XPS) and generate a detectable amount of CO2 reduction products (e.g., CO) under identical reaction conditions.
fields.baseline: Standard Mo2C catalysts that, upon immersion in aqueous media, form a stable ~1 ML MoO2-like layer and exclusively catalyze the HER.
fields.boundary: This hypothesis applies to conditions where the protective layer remains intact (i.e., under moderate overpotentials and in the absence of aggressive oxidation agents) and where the overlayer thickness is optimized to not block electron transfer.
fields.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in finding the optimal thickness/composition of the carbon overlayer that balances protection with catalytic conductivity, and whether the layer might introduce additional resistance or hinder mass transfer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mo2C films: one with an ultrathin carbon overlayer and one uncoated. Under identical aqueous electrolyte conditions and polarization, perform XPS to assess oxide thickness and use product analysis (via DEMS and GC) to detect CO2RR specific products. Additionally, carry out electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to check for changes in charge transfer resistance due to coating.
measurements: XPS for surface composition/oxide thickness
Electrochemical product distribution (DEMS/GC)
EIS for conductivity differences
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon coated Mo2C does not show a reduction in oxide formation and the CO2RR product yield remains comparable to the uncoated sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

fields.hypothesis: A controlled electrochemical pre-oxidation treatment that tunes the surface oxidation state distribution—enhancing Co3+ and Fe2+ content—will improve the durability and selectivity of transition-metal oxide catalysts during OER.
fields.material_initial_state: A standard transition-metal oxide catalyst (e.g., CoFe oxide) with a conventional, mixed surface oxidation state distribution.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (via potential pulses in an alkaline electrolyte) to adjust the surface chemistry, selectively increasing the proportion of Co3+ and Fe2+ active centers.
fields.conditions: Side-by-side electrochemical testing under identical alkaline OER conditions comparing pre-oxidized catalysts with untreated controls; monitoring both short-term activity and long-term durability.
fields.structural_mediator: The formation of a tailored surface layer—likely in the form of (M)OOH species—with an optimized balance of divalent/trivalent sites enhances electron transfer and stabilizes intermediate adsorption.
fields.mechanism: Altering the oxidation state favors the formation of oxyhydroxide phases that assist in the adsorption and conversion of OER intermediates; higher Co3+ levels can boost kinetics while increased Fe2+ content can stabilize active sites against dissolution, similar to the paper’s observed surface state benefits in HEOs.
fields.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized catalysts are expected to exhibit a lower onset potential and a reduced rate of performance degradation (smaller increases in overpotential over time) compared to untreated catalysts.
fields.baseline: Catalysts identical in synthesis that do not receive the pre-oxidation treatment.
fields.boundary: The benefits should manifest in alkaline electrolytes and within moderate potential ranges where surface oxidation can be finely controlled without over-oxidizing the material.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal treatment parameters (e.g., potential, duration) and exact oxidation state ratios for peak performance are not precisely known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of CoFe oxide catalysts, one undergoing a controlled pre-oxidation treatment and one remaining untreated. Use XPS to quantify surface oxidation states before and after treatment, then perform extended OER cycling tests.
measurements: Changes in oxidation state ratios via XPS (e.g., Co3+/Co2+ and Fe2+/Fe3+)
Overpotential stability over time
Faradaic efficiency
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized catalysts do not demonstrate an improved durability profile (i.e., smaller overpotential increases) or show no significant change in surface oxidation state compared to controls, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: the paper's finding that IrV=O formation is a key resting state in the OER mechanism, as revealed by in situ XAS and DFT
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the concept by investigating how the electronic nature of the support itself can be tuned to modulate high-valent intermediate stabilization, rather than solely focusing on the metal site chemistry.

fields.hypothesis: Catalytic activity in single‐atom transition‐metal catalysts is governed by the ability of the oxide support to stabilize high‐valent metal–oxo (M=O) intermediates. Supports with more electrophilic or strongly interacting oxide surfaces enhance the formation and stabilization of the M=O intermediate, thereby lowering the reaction overpotential.
fields.material_initial_state: Atomically dispersed Ir on In₂O₃/SnO₂ (ITO) as used in the baseline study.
fields.intervention: Prepare analogous single‐atom catalysts using alternative conductive oxide supports (e.g., SnO₂, TiO₂, or doped ITO) that have different electronic properties to modulate the metal–support interaction.
fields.conditions: Conduct oxygen evolution reaction (OER) testing in 0.1 M HClO₄ under identical catalytic loadings and electrochemical measurement protocols as in the baseline experiment.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation and stabilization of high‐valent M=O species, as monitored by in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) showing metal–oxo distances near 1.8–1.83 Å.
fields.mechanism: Different oxide supports influence the electron density at the metal site. Supports that promote stronger metal–support electronic coupling can stabilize the high‐valent M=O intermediate (analogous to the observed IrV=O in the paper), leading to more facile proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) steps and lower overpotentials.
fields.predicted_outcome: Catalysts on supports with more favorable electronic interactions are predicted to exhibit a modest reduction in onset potential (e.g., around 10–20 mV lower overpotential) and higher current per metal site compared to baseline IrSAC–ITO.
fields.baseline: IrSAC–ITO catalyst as prepared and characterized in PMC7379386.
fields.boundary: This mechanism should apply under acidic OER conditions where the support is inert and the high‐valent oxo formation is rate‐determining; effects may differ if the support’s conductivity or surface area changes significantly.
fields.uncertainty: Exact quantitative shifts in overpotential are uncertain due to possible interplay of additional factors like surface area and hydrophilicity.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize single-atom catalysts on at least three different oxide supports (e.g., standard ITO, SnO₂, and TiO₂) with equivalent metal loadings. Under identical OER conditions, record steady-state voltammetry and perform in situ XAS to assess the metal–oxo bond lengths.
measurements: Overpotential at defined current densities
In situ XAS to determine metal–oxo bond distances
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If catalysts on alternative supports do not show systematic differences in the stabilization (i.e., bond lengths) of the high-valent M=O intermediate and similar overpotential changes relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C6

pool.what_is_new: This proposal introduces the strategy of support doping to enhance the anchoring of single-metal centers, thereby addressing durability issues not resolved in the original work.

fields.hypothesis: Durability of single-atom catalysts under OER conditions is governed by the anchoring strength between the transition-metal centers and the oxide support; enhancing these anchoring sites via support doping will reduce metal migration and aggregation, thereby improving catalyst stability.
fields.material_initial_state: Atomically dispersed Ir on ITO (IrSAC–ITO), which under prolonged high-current operation shows some migration to form small clusters.
fields.intervention: Dope the ITO support with a small amount of tungsten (or another high-valent metal) to introduce stronger binding (anchoring) sites for the Ir atoms.
fields.conditions: Carry out OER in 0.1 M HClO₄ under identical conditions and current densities (including prolonged electrolysis at 10 mA cm⁻²) as for the undoped baseline.
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced formation of Ir–O–W bonds at defect or doping sites, which immobilize Ir atoms and prevent their surface migration.
fields.mechanism: The tungsten dopant creates more robust anchoring sites on the oxide support. This increased interaction prevents the diffusion and aggregation of the active Ir sites during extended OER operation, thereby maintaining high catalytic activity and durability.
fields.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-doped catalyst is expected to show a significantly improved durability (e.g., stable overpotential over extended testing) and a higher fraction of isolated Ir atoms (as confirmed by HAADF-STEM) compared to undoped IrSAC–ITO.
fields.baseline: Standard IrSAC–ITO catalyst as reported in PMC7379386, which exhibits partial aggregation after prolonged operation.
fields.boundary: The improved durability mechanism is expected to hold under acidic OER conditions and when metal mobility is a major degradation route; if other degradation mechanisms dominate, the effect may be limited.

fields.hypothesis: Pulsed anodic oxidation of Ni thin films will create discrete, nanoscale Ni(OH)2 islands embedded in a matrix of metallic Ni, thereby multiplying the beneficial metal–hydroxide interfaces that optimize hydrogen adsorption kinetics during HER.
fields.material_initial_state: Ultra-smooth, nanocrystalline sputtered Ni thin films with a native, non-uniform oxide layer.
fields.intervention: Replace the continuous, steady anodic oxidation step with a pulsed potential oxidation protocol (e.g., alternating short anodic pulses with rest intervals in 1 M KOH) to promote nucleation of isolated Ni(OH)2 islands rather than uniform oxide coverage.
fields.conditions: Alkaline HER conditions (1 M KOH, room temperature) in a three‐electrode cell, with potential pulses carefully controlled (pulse amplitude and duration) to tailor oxidation extent.
fields.structural_mediator: Spatially isolated Ni(OH)2 islands interspersed with unoxidized Ni ensure high density of Ni0/Ni(OH)2 interfaces without complete surface passivation.
fields.mechanism: The pulsed potential sequence limits the diffusion and growth of oxide, encouraging heterogeneous nucleation that produces numerous interfacial sites. These interfaces adjust hydrogen binding energies by locally altering electronic states (lowering activation energy for Volmer–Heyrovsky steps), hence enhancing HER kinetics. This builds on the paper’s insight that mixed Ni/Ni(OH)2 phases boost catalytic activity (PMC10383487::web::003::1_introduction) while addressing the challenge of uncontrolled oxide thickness.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to films oxidized under steady potentials, the pulsed-oxidized films should show a statistically significant lower overpotential at a given current density and a higher exchange current density (potentially in a similar 3–5× range as observed for overall oxidation but with even better interfacial control).
fields.baseline: As-deposited Ni thin films and films oxidized by conventional continuous anodic polarization.
fields.boundary: The effect is expected to be valid for ultrathin, smooth Ni films under alkaline conditions; its applicability in rougher films or different pH media may differ.
fields.uncertainty: Precise pulse parameters for optimal island size/density need calibration; quantitative improvements over conventional oxidation are subject to experimental variability.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pulsed-oxidized films do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in HER metrics or do not show a distinct, controllable interfacial pattern compared to continuous oxidation, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.what_is_new: This proposal introduces the strategy of support doping to enhance the anchoring of single-metal centers, thereby addressing durability issues not resolved in the original work.

fields.hypothesis: Durability of single-atom catalysts under OER conditions is governed by the anchoring strength between the transition-metal centers and the oxide support; enhancing these anchoring sites via support doping will reduce metal migration and aggregation, thereby improving catalyst stability.
fields.material_initial_state: Atomically dispersed Ir on ITO (IrSAC–ITO), which under prolonged high-current operation shows some migration to form small clusters.
fields.intervention: Dope the ITO support with a small amount of tungsten (or another high-valent metal) to introduce stronger binding (anchoring) sites for the Ir atoms.
fields.conditions: Carry out OER in 0.1 M HClO₄ under identical conditions and current densities (including prolonged electrolysis at 10 mA cm⁻²) as for the undoped baseline.
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced formation of Ir–O–W bonds at defect or doping sites, which immobilize Ir atoms and prevent their surface migration.
fields.mechanism: The tungsten dopant creates more robust anchoring sites on the oxide support. This increased interaction prevents the diffusion and aggregation of the active Ir sites during extended OER operation, thereby maintaining high catalytic activity and durability.
fields.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-doped catalyst is expected to show a significantly improved durability (e.g., stable overpotential over extended testing) and a higher fraction of isolated Ir atoms (as confirmed by HAADF-STEM) compared to undoped IrSAC–ITO.
fields.baseline: Standard IrSAC–ITO catalyst as reported in PMC7379386, which exhibits partial aggregation after prolonged operation.
fields.boundary: The improved durability mechanism is expected to hold under acidic OER conditions and when metal mobility is a major degradation route; if other degradation mechanisms dominate, the effect may be limited.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal dopant concentration and the magnitude of durability improvement remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one on undoped ITO and one on tungsten-doped ITO, ensuring similar Ir loadings and initial dispersion. Carry out long-term chronoamperometry at high current density (10 mA cm⁻²) and subsequently perform HAADF-STEM imaging to evaluate the degree of Ir aggregation.
measurements: Overpotential stability over time
HAADF-STEM quantification of isolated atoms vs. clusters
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped catalysts do not show marked improvement in long-term overpotential stability and if post-operation imaging reveals similar or higher levels of aggregation compared to the undoped control, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C3
top3.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration that oxide formation at the Mo2C surface is the key detrimental factor for CO2RR activity.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a protective coating strategy to physically inhibit oxidation while preserving catalyst functionality — a route not investigated in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A deliberately applied ultrathin carbon protective overlayer on Mo2C will act as a diffusion barrier against oxygen, thereby mitigating the formation of passivating surface oxides and preserving the catalyst’s intrinsic CO2RR activity in aqueous media.
fields.material_initial_state: Air-exposed Mo2C films that rapidly form MoO2-like surface oxides upon immersion in aqueous electrolytes.
fields.intervention: Deposit an ultrathin, conductive carbon layer (via chemical vapor deposition or pyrolysis of a carbon precursor) atop the Mo2C catalyst immediately after synthesis, ensuring minimal thickness to allow electron transfer while hampering oxygen infiltration.
fields.conditions: Aqueous electrolyte (e.g., 0.1 M KHCO3 at pH ~6.9) with typical cathodic polarization conditions for CO2 reduction.
fields.structural_mediator: A conformal nanometer-scale carbon film that adheres to the Mo2C surface and modulates the interfacial chemistry by limiting oxygen diffusion without significantly impeding charge transport.
fields.mechanism: The protective carbon overlayer is expected to prevent or slow the ingress of oxygen species during exposure to aqueous electrolyte. This reduction in oxide formation maintains the active carbide surface that is predicted (by prior DFT studies and indicated in the paper) to have favorable adsorption properties for CO2 and its intermediates, thereby shifting the reaction selectivity away from HER toward CO2RR.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to uncoated Mo2C that rapidly forms HER-active oxide films, the coated catalyst should show a markedly thinner oxide film (as measured by XPS) and generate a detectable amount of CO2 reduction products (e.g., CO) under identical reaction conditions.
fields.baseline: Standard Mo2C catalysts that, upon immersion in aqueous media, form a stable ~1 ML MoO2-like layer and exclusively catalyze the HER.
fields.boundary: This hypothesis applies to conditions where the protective layer remains intact (i.e., under moderate overpotentials and in the absence of aggressive oxidation agents) and where the overlayer thickness is optimized to not block electron transfer.
fields.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in finding the optimal thickness/composition of the carbon overlayer that balances protection with catalytic conductivity, and whether the layer might introduce additional resistance or hinder mass transfer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mo2C films: one with an ultrathin carbon overlayer and one uncoated. Under identical aqueous electrolyte conditions and polarization, perform XPS to assess oxide thickness and use product analysis (via DEMS and GC) to detect CO2RR specific products. Additionally, carry out electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to check for changes in charge transfer resistance due to coating.
measurements: XPS for surface composition/oxide thickness
Electrochemical product distribution (DEMS/GC)
EIS for conductivity differences
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon coated Mo2C does not show a reduction in oxide formation and the CO2RR product yield remains comparable to the uncoated sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.
